subject: Culture
title: Seating Order Politics
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Seating Order Politics.

hook.text: At a Chinese banquet, the guest of honor sits facing the door. It's not random—it's protocol.

buildup.text: Seating order reveals power. In medieval Europe, proximity to the king determined your status.

discovery.text: The phrase 'above the salt' comes from when the salt cellar separated nobles from commoners at the table.

twist.text: In egalitarian Scandinavian cultures, assigned seating feels forced. Everyone mixes freely.

climax.text: Where you sit at the table can honor you, test you, or put you in your place.

punchline.text: The chair is a political statement.

quiz.question: What did the phrase 'above the salt' originally indicate?
options: Higher social status at the table

details.summary: Where you sit at a table communicates power, status, and social relationships in every culture. Chinese banquets place the guest of honor facing the door. Medieval European lords sat at raised high tables. Japanese seating follows strict seniority. A chair's position is never just practical.
details.whyItMatters: Seating politics are invisible to cultural outsiders but obvious to insiders. Sitting in the wrong place at a formal dinner can be as offensive as a verbal insult.
takeaways: Chinese banquet seating places the host with their back to the door
Medieval high tables physically elevated the lord above guests
Japanese kamiza seating follows strict hierarchical rules

faq.question: How does Chinese banquet seating work?
faq.answer: The guest of honor sits facing the door (the position of security and visibility). The host sits opposite, with their back to the door (showing trust by being vulnerable). Seating radiates outward from these positions in order of status.

faq.question: What is Japanese kamiza?
faq.answer: Kamiza is the seat of honor — typically the spot farthest from the entrance, often in front of the tokonoma (decorative alcove). The most junior person sits nearest the door (shimoza) to serve others and handle interruptions.
